text: A third of manufacturing workers are over 50, but Level 4+ technician training is thin, risking a skills cliff-edge.
Curriculum often lags new technology - employers describe apprentices trained on outdated kit and old course titles.
89% of manufacturing firms are micro-businesses, so most can't run in-house training and need coordinated brokerage.
56% of manufacturing sites with vacancies say they are hard to fill, and 39% are skill-shortage vacancies.
70% of the farming workforce is over 50, just as robotics and precision technology are taking off.
Robotics and data skills are mostly learned informally on the job, with almost no formal training pathway yet.
Rural transport gaps make it hard for young people to reach the FE and apprenticeship provision that already exists.
Demand is shifting fast from routine admin roles toward analytical, digital and AI-literate roles.
Local wages often can't match Manchester's, so the region struggles to retain the graduates it trains.
Level 4-5 pathways into data, compliance and digital business analyst roles are underdeveloped.
50% of clean-energy-type vacancies are hard to fill and 35% are skill-shortage vacancies.
Courses on hydrogen and other emerging technologies barely exist yet, so there's no clear training route in.
Major projects like HyNet risk competing for the same small pool of skilled workers at the same time.
36% of the energy and water workforce is over 50, adding replacement pressure on top of growth.
Level 4-5 technician pathways into lab science and pharmaceutical manufacturing are underdeveloped.
Employers rarely engage with schools and colleges, so students don't see non-graduate routes into the sector.
Colleges launched Lab Skills bootcamps, but too few employers show up to interview the graduates.
Apprenticeship completions run at only around 49%, so training starts aren't converting into site-ready workers.
Level 4+ apprenticeships make up just 10% of local construction enrolments, limiting supervisory pathways.
Over 95% of apprenticeship starts are male, showing construction still isn't reaching everyone it could.
Retrofit work needs whole-house and quality-assurance skills that go beyond traditional trade training.
Only around 31% of FE health and care enrolments turn into completed achievements, the lowest conversion of any sector.
Just 110 Level 4+ enrolments locally means a very thin pipeline for supervisors and registered managers.
Registered managers are in such short supply that one care home paid a £16,000 agency fee for a single hire.
Only 19% of direct care workers hold a Level 2 relevant social care qualification.
